title: I Applied the Blood-Drive Snack Cap to the Coordinator Who Set It

parts.text: I clocked into the blood-drive gym at 7:41 a.m. and the snack table was already a fortress of granola the coordinator had reserved with a sticky: STAFF ONLY UNTIL 11. The laminated cap she signed said: DONOR SNACKS FIRST. TWO ITEMS. NO STAFF HOLD. I was twenty-eight, phlebotomy assistant, holding a fainting donor who needed juice now. Mara, the coordinator, palmed three juices into a tote labeled TRAINING. "Staff fuel," she said. I pointed at her own cap. She laughed. "Coordinators are donors of time." I photographed the tote, the cap, and the donor's empty cup. Then I moved the tote to the public table and logged a donor-care note. At 7:58 the charge nurse asked why Mara's name was on a snack-diversion ticket.
parts.cliffhanger_hint: The charge nurse can see Mara's tote on the donor table with the cap she signed.

social.video_title: She hoarded the juice under a staff sticky — Part 1/2
social.description: Blood drive, a coordinator's tote, and a snack cap she laminated herself. I logged the diversion. Would you have moved the tote?

parts.text: Mara called it a joke until the donor asked for the snack log. I printed the ticket, the cap, and the photo. Nutrition restocked the juice. Mara ate a crushed granola bar in the hallway and told volunteers the cap was always about optics. Optics is a word coordinators use when a photo exists. Snack policy now has a second line: COORDINATORS ARE NOT DONORS OF THE JUICE. I keep two cups on a labeled tray. Mara brown-bags. The table finally looks like a clinic, not a pantry.

social.description: Snack log, charge nurse, and a second line on the cap. Was training ever a fainting donor?
